summary.prose: A developer sees and edits their own tracker settings for a repo (tracker type, target, the gh tool location, the host gh signs in to, and branch naming) in VS Code, JetBrains and the terminal client. Sign-in itself is shown as a live read-only status, because insrc stores no secrets: by the owner's recorded decision this is how 'edit sign-in' in the upstream criteria is met. The team's policy rules appear next to the settings as read-only values. All three clients render the same rows from one daemon definition, and the daemon is the only process that writes ~/.insrc/github.json, so a change made in one client shows in the others and writers cannot overwrite each other.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: A daemon-side team gate over a synchronous, capability-declaring tracker port (alternative a1). The port (sc1) is the only way the workflow library talks to a tracker; GitHub is its first adapter, made by extracting the existing GitHub code (src/workflow/tracker, the issue calls in tracker-auto.ts, and the create and close calls in src/workflow/bugfix/tracker.ts) behind it. sc1 is the one tracker abstraction: the unbuilt tracker-tool design (LLD-38436e90625a83a2-S001) is not built as a second abstraction and is superseded or amended by s1's LLD. The policy (sc2) is read from the remote default branch and says which stages need signoff, whether claims are enforced, the claim units and the administrators. The artifact's tracker record keeps every existing meta.tracker field exactly as it is and gains additive per-unit data, plus an optional meta.revision (sc3). The team gate (sc4) takes a guarded action and returns an outcome. Signoff is a separate record (sc5) that never changes meta.review or approvedAt. Syncing tracker status on git pull and push, and the issue-status read it needs, are deferred with the later-tracker work to a define extend and are not part of this HLD.

nonFunctional.performance: Each guarded action makes at most two live reads through the port (the signed-in user and the assignee); every tracker command has a 10-second timeout, after which the action is refused with the reason. A repo without a policy makes no tracker call.
nonFunctional.security: Policy is read only from the remote default branch ref and is not locally overridable; enforcement lives in the daemon-owned workflow library (k1); no tracker secrets are stored by insrc, sign-in stays with the tracker's CLI; administrators come only from the policy.
nonFunctional.observability: Every gate outcome other than allowed is logged with unit, action and reason; port failures carry their kind (missing-tool, missing-signin, unreachable, rejected).
nonFunctional.durability: Claim, issue and signoff state live in the tracker and in committed artifact files; the in-memory step state stores (100 entries, 1 hour) are not relied on for handoff. Artifact writes stay atomic through the existing helper.

dataModelChanges.details: The one definition table of the repo-scoped rows, in src/config next to CONFIG_CATALOG. Each row: key, label, type (string | boolean | enum), enumValues, default, description, group Tracker, optional note, optional grammar, and kind: local (editable, stored in github.json), status (derived, read-only: sign-in status and the resolved target with its source) or policy (read-only, from sc2). Local rows: type (github | none), owner, repo, ghPath, ghHost (default github.com), branchPattern; ghPath, ghHost and branchPattern carry the note 'saved; not used yet'. The branchPattern row carries its grammar, which is the single definition that the validator and, later, s6 read: the only placeholders are {id}, {slug} and {type}; any other brace token, an unmatched brace or a literal brace is rejected and there is no escaping; every other character is a letter, digit, slash, hyphen, underscore or dot; the pattern is 1 to 200 characters, does not start or end with a slash, has no two consecutive slashes, no '..' and does not end with '.lock'. s6 may extend the grammar only by changing this row. Policy rows, one per team rule in TeamPolicy: teamMode, signoffStages, claimsEnforced, claimUnits, administrators, forceTaskIssues. Accepted interpretation (owner decision, 2026-10-17, recorded in docs/plans/team-workflow.md): 'edit sign-in' (ac10, ac11) is met by a read-only sign-in status row plus the editable ghHost row.

{ repo: string; values: Record<string, string | boolean>; resolved: { type: 'github' | 'none'; owner?: string; repo?: string; source: 'per-repo-config' | 'default-config' | 'git-remote'; error?: string }; signin: { state: 'signed-in' | 'missing-tool' | 'missing-signin' | 'unreachable' | 'rejected' | 'disabled'; login?: string; reason?: string }; policy: { ok: true; mode: 'none' } | { ok: true; mode: 'team'; values: Record<string, unknown>; source: { ref: string; fetchedAt: string } } | { ok: false; reason: string } }. values holds only keys the repo's own entry sets; policy.values has one entry per policy row.

WriteError is { code: 'github-json-unreadable' | 'file-changed' | 'write-failed'; message: string }. RepoSettingsError is { code: WriteError['code'] | 'unknown-key' | 'read-only-key' | 'invalid-value' | 'repo-not-registered'; message: string } returned as { ok: false, error }. JetBrains maps ok:false to SaveResult.Rejected(message) (or RepoSettingsResult.Rejected) and a transport fault to Unavailable; VS Code maps it to ConfigWriteResult { ok: false, reason: message }; the terminal client shows the message; the tracker setup config step reports a failed step with the message as detail.

errorCases.scenario: github.json is unreadable: it cannot be read, is not valid JSON, has a top level that is not an object, has default or repos present and not an object, or has the repo's own entry present and null, an array or a primitive
errorCases.detection: readRepoEntry reads the file and parses it with JSON.parse without swallowing errors (unlike loadGithubConfigFile), then checks each level in order with a plain-object test: the top level, then default when present, then repos when present, then the selected entry when present; the first failing level or the read or parse error is named in the reason.
errorCases.response: repo.settings.get, repo.settings.set and repo.trackerConfig.ensure return { ok: false, error: { code: 'github-json-unreadable', message } } naming the file and the failing level; the writer writes nothing and leaves the file byte for byte unchanged. Because repo.settings.get resolves from the snapshot it just validated, the TypeError resolveEntry would throw for a null entry cannot be reached.
errorCases.userImpact: The client shows the error and where to fix the file by hand; no setting is lost, and a malformed file is never shown as 'no tracker'.

errorCases.scenario: Tracker setup in the terminal meets a structurally malformed github.json (a null own entry while the default is complete, a null default, a non-object top level, default or repos, or invalid JSON)
errorCases.detection: planTrackerConfig calls the strict readRepoEntry before anything else. The lenient loader and the selection file.repos?.[repo] ?? file.default are not used for the decision, so a null own entry cannot fall through to a complete default and a null default is never dereferenced.
errorCases.response: planTrackerConfig returns failed with the strict reader's message naming the failing level; trackerSetup passes that as a failed configOutcome, never calls the daemon for the config step and writes nothing; the remaining setup steps still run.
errorCases.userImpact: Setup reports the config step failed with the exact problem in the file instead of reporting it already configured.

errorCases.scenario: A branchPattern value breaks the grammar: a brace token other than {id}, {slug} or {type}, an unmatched or literal brace, a character outside letters, digits, slash, hyphen, underscore and dot, a length outside 1 to 200, a leading or trailing slash, two consecutive slashes, '..', or a '.lock' ending
errorCases.detection: repo.settings.set validates the value against the grammar defined on the branchPattern row of REPO_TRACKER_FIELDS before any file access: it scans for brace tokens and compares each with the three allowed placeholders, then checks the remaining characters and the structural rules.
errorCases.response: Returns invalid-value naming the rule that failed; nothing is written.
errorCases.userImpact: The client shows which rule the pattern broke and keeps the old value.

errorCases.scenario: github.json is changed by another process while repo.settings.get is working
errorCases.detection: There is no second read: the strict reader reads once, validates, and the target is resolved from that same in-memory snapshot.
errorCases.response: The call returns the values and resolved target of the version it read; a later change is picked up by the next get.
errorCases.userImpact: A client may show a value a moment old; never a half-updated mixture.

errorCases.scenario: Two clients write at about the same time through the daemon (for example VS Code and JetBrains, or a settings edit and a tracker setup)
errorCases.detection: All writes reach writeRepoEntryKeys inside the one daemon process, which chains each call on a single in-process promise queue, so a second call starts only after the first has finished or failed.
errorCases.response: The writes apply one after the other; each reads the file at its start and merges into the latest content, so both edits survive. There is no lock file, no wait limit and no file-locked error. A failure of one write does not stall the queue.
errorCases.userImpact: Both edits are kept; the second client sees the first client's value afterwards.

errorCases.scenario: A process outside the daemon (an editor, a script, a leftover older terminal build) changes github.json while a write is in progress
errorCases.detection: The verify step: immediately before the rename the writer re-reads the file and compares size, mtime and content hash with those it recorded when it read.
errorCases.response: The attempt restarts from the new content; after the fixed number of attempts the write is refused with file-changed and nothing is written. An edit that lands between the final check and the rename cannot be detected, because rename cannot be made conditional; this is the one stated limit and it concerns only processes that are not the daemon.
errorCases.userImpact: An outside edit can still be lost in a very small window; the design does not claim to prevent it.

errorCases.scenario: The daemon is not running or not reachable when the terminal client runs tracker setup
errorCases.detection: trackerSetup awaits repo.trackerConfig.ensure through rpc with timeoutMs 15000; connecting to a missing socket rejects through rpc's existing error handling.
errorCases.response: The config step is reported failed with a detail that says the daemon owns ~/.insrc/github.json and must be running, and the remaining setup steps still run and report as they do today. Nothing is written by the terminal process.
errorCases.userImpact: The developer is told to start the daemon and run setup again; labels and other steps are not blocked.

errorCases.scenario: The daemon accepts the socket but never replies, or closes the connection without replying
errorCases.detection: With opts.timeoutMs set, rpc starts a deadline timer when the request is sent and listens for the socket's end and close events; the timer firing, or end or close arriving before a reply has been parsed, rejects the promise.
errorCases.response: rpc destroys the socket and clears the timer on every outcome; trackerSetup catches the rejection and reports the config step failed with a timed-out or connection-closed message that says the daemon owns the file; the other setup steps still run. Calls made without opts.timeoutMs behave exactly as before.
errorCases.userImpact: Setup finishes within the deadline and says why the config step failed; it never hangs.

errorCases.scenario: A caller runs runTrackerSetup without the config seam outside a test (a mistake that would reintroduce a second writer)
errorCases.detection: A test builds the real terminal services with makeServices and asserts that its trackerSetup passes configOutcome into runTrackerSetup in every branch (already, needs-write succeeded, needs-write failed, plan failed, daemon unreachable, timed out), and a search test fails if production code outside the daemon and the tests calls runTrackerSetup without it.
errorCases.response: The build fails the test; the in-process default stays reachable only from tests and in-process callers.
errorCases.userImpact: No second writer of github.json ships.

errorCases.scenario: A filesystem failure while writing the temporary file or renaming it (permission denied, missing directory, read-only disk, disk full)
errorCases.detection: writeRepoEntryKeys wraps the temporary write and the rename in one try block and catches the operating-system error code (EACCES, EPERM, ENOENT, ENOSPC, EROFS, EXDEV).
errorCases.response: The temporary file is removed, the target file is left as it was, and the call returns write-failed with the operating-system message; the queue continues.
errorCases.userImpact: The client shows the operating-system reason and nothing is changed.

errorCases.scenario: A client sends a write for a policy or status row
errorCases.detection: repo.settings.set looks the key up in REPO_TRACKER_FIELDS and checks kind is local.
errorCases.userImpact: The row is shown read-only in every client, so this only happens from a hand-made call (k5).

errorCases.scenario: A value does not match its row (an enum outside its values, an owner or repo that is not a valid GitHub name, a ghPath or ghHost that contains a newline)
errorCases.detection: repo.settings.set and repo.trackerConfig.ensure validate the value against the row's type, enumValues and format before any file access.
errorCases.response: Returns invalid-value with the reason; nothing is written.
errorCases.userImpact: The client shows the reason next to the field and keeps the old value.

errorCases.scenario: The repo is not registered with the daemon, or the path given is an alias (for example a symlink or a path with a trailing slash) that is not the registered string
errorCases.detection: The daemon methods compare the given path with the registered repo paths as repo.add stored them (resolve(path), no symlink resolution) before reading or writing.
errorCases.response: Returns repo-not-registered; no file is read or written. A symlink and its target that were both registered by the user are two repos with two entries, exactly as the registry and resolveGithubConfig already treat them; this story adds no alias lookup, merge or migration.
errorCases.userImpact: The client picker only lists registered repos by their registered path, so the error appears only after a repo is removed while the settings are open.

errorCases.scenario: The policy cannot be read (offline, no default branch known, malformed policy file)
errorCases.detection: PolicyReader returns ok:false and repo.settings.get checks the result.
errorCases.response: The payload carries policy: { ok: false, reason }; the local rows are still returned.
errorCases.userImpact: The policy section shows the reason instead of values; editing the local rows is unaffected.

errorCases.scenario: The sign-in status check fails: gh missing, not signed in (including an empty login), timed out, or rejected for another reason
errorCases.detection: repo.settings.get calls whoAmI on the s1 adapter (sc1) and switches on the PortResult: ok gives signed-in with the login; ok:false maps its kind one to one onto signin.state and copies the reason; an exception thrown by the adapter is caught and reported as rejected with the message.
errorCases.response: signin.state and signin.reason are set and the call still succeeds; it uses the adapter's 10-second timeout and is not retried.
errorCases.userImpact: The sign-in row says exactly what is wrong without blocking the settings view. The row is a status only, by the owner's recorded decision of 2026-10-17.

errorCases.scenario: github is enabled for the repo but no target can be resolved
errorCases.detection: resolveGithubConfigFromFile throws GithubConfigError, caught in repo.settings.get after the structural validation passes.
errorCases.response: resolved.error carries the message and resolved.type is none; the call succeeds and no sign-in check runs (signin.state disabled).
errorCases.userImpact: The target row shows why there is no target and which fields to set.

errorCases.scenario: An older client calls config.catalog and does not know repoFields, or a newer client talks to an older daemon that omits repoFields
errorCases.detection: The field is additive; the new VS Code gateway maps a missing repoFields to an empty list and the Kotlin DTO field defaults to an empty list.
errorCases.response: No change for existing fields; the tracker section is simply empty or absent.
errorCases.userImpact: The tracker section appears only when both the client and the daemon are updated.

errorCases.scenario: A repo's settings cannot be loaded in the JetBrains settings page
errorCases.detection: InsrcSettingsConfigurable calls readRepoSettings per registered repo on its pooled thread and receives Rejected or Unavailable for that repo.
errorCases.response: The page still renders; PerRepoSection shows that reason in place of the tracker rows of that repo and keeps the model-tier rows working.
errorCases.userImpact: One repo's tracker section shows why it is empty; the rest of the page is unaffected.

alternativesConsidered.name: Daemon as the only writer of github.json, serialised in process, validated planning and a bounded setup request
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: A single field table in src/config describes the repo-scoped rows and is exposed through config.catalog; the daemon alone writes github.json through one in-process queue; the terminal tracker setup validates the file structure before planning, asks the daemon with a bounded request, and never writes the file itself; all three clients render from the payload.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add one definition site, a REPO_TRACKER_FIELDS table next to CONFIG_CATALOG, with rows of kind local, status and policy; buildSettingsCatalog exposes it as a static repoFields field, and the branchPattern row carries the grammar that the validator and s6 share. Add daemon methods repo.settings.get(repo), repo.settings.set(repo, key, value) and repo.trackerConfig.ensure(repo, owner, name). The github.json module has a strict reader and writeRepoEntryKeys. Because only the daemon process writes the file, writes are serialised by an in-process queue (no lock file, no reclaim, no file-locked error); inside a write the daemon reads, validates, merges, writes a temp file, verifies size, mtime and content hash again and renames, retrying a bounded number of times for edits by outside processes. repo.settings.get validates once and resolves from the same snapshot through resolveGithubConfigFromFile. Repo identity is the exact registered path string. Sign-in is a live read-only status from whoAmI on s1's adapter (sc1), read only and never changing tracker state; the editable part is ghHost (owner-approved reading). Terminal setup: the pure planTrackerConfig first runs the strict readRepoEntry on the file and turns any validation failure (unreadable file, a null or non-object own entry even when a default is complete, a null default, non-object levels) into a failed outcome carrying the strict reader's message; only a structurally valid file reaches the completeness test, so a malformed file is never reported as already and nothing can dereference null. When a write is needed the terminal service awaits repo.trackerConfig.ensure through the shared rpc with a bounded request: rpc gains an opt-in fourth parameter { timeoutMs } that rejects on the deadline and on the socket ending or closing before a reply and always destroys the socket; calls without it behave exactly as today, so the VS Code extension and other callers are unchanged. A timeout or early close makes the config step failed with a message that the daemon owns the file and must be running, and the remaining setup steps still run. runTrackerSetup takes an optional configOutcome seam, trackerSetup is asynchronous, and a test proves the terminal service always injects the seam. sighting-store.ts is not touched. Host wiring is as in the previous revision: JetBrains forwards, doubles and the DTO default with its five tests; VS Code snapshot, renderer and handler dependencies, webview message, seam test and the FakeGateway, model-tier-picker, detail-renderers, repo-config and activation tests; the terminal client Services members, async trackerSetup and settings modal.
pros: One definition of the fields, so the three clients cannot drift
No cross-process lock, so no reclaim race and no stale lock
A malformed file can never be reported as already configured
A silent or crashed daemon cannot hang tracker setup
The rpc change is opt-in, so existing callers are unaffected
The branchPattern grammar is defined once, where s6 will read it
cons: Tracker setup needs the daemon for its config step and trackerSetup becomes asynchronous
Reverses the earlier owner answer to question 4, recorded in the plan document
Edits by processes outside the daemon are only detected on a best-effort basis
s3 depends on s1's adapter (sc1) for the sign-in status, which the HLD boundary for s3 does not list
About thirty-eight files change across the daemon, shared client, three clients and fixtures

alternativesConsidered.name: Generalise config.catalog and config.write with a store selector
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Keep one catalog and one write method and add a store dimension so the same calls address github.json per-repo entries as well as config.json.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Extend ConfigOption with an optional scope of repo and a store of github.json, add a repoPath parameter to config.catalog and config.write, and branch inside buildSettingsCatalog and the write handler on the store. Repo rows live in CONFIG_CATALOG beside the daemon-wide rows. Policy rows are added to the same payload with a read-only flag.
pros: Smallest client change if they already render the catalog generically
One pair of methods for every setting
cons: config.write is global and path-based; widening it risks corrupting config.json
The catalog is pure and total; reading a second file and the policy breaks that
Couples the catalog to the policy reader
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Closest to literal k6 but widens a global write path and breaks the purity and totality of the catalog (partial on ac12-ac14, sc2 and k4).

alternativesConsidered.name: Each client owns its tracker form and talks to github.json through a thin read and write
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Add only a raw read and write of a repo entry to the daemon and let each client define its own fields and validation.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add repo.githubEntry.get and repo.githubEntry.set that move the entry JSON as is, with the daemon checking only that it is an object. VS Code, JetBrains and the terminal client each hard-code the tracker fields, labels and validation.
pros: Clients lay the form out as suits their toolkit
cons: Three copies of the field list and validation, which is the drift the story forbids
A client bug can write an entry the strict resolver refuses
Policy values need a third method and per-client handling
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Violates the one-definition rule (k6) and leaves validation to three clients.
